scope: 44 people, 55 relationships and 81 chronicle events spanning 209 BCE to 2024. All original 32 people, 53 relationships and 18 initial events are retained. Twelve cross-period biographies add directly sourced person entry points to 17 events.
method: Read English and Cyrillic-Mongolian Wikipedia biographies/sections; compare only the facts named in each row. Interlanguage agreement is not independent historical proof. Preserve stronger existing sources when coverage differs.
languageReview: Event, navigation and new-person drafts are enumerated in history-copy-draft.json. Targeted dictionary corrections are separate from complete sentence proofreading; no Menksoft or native-language completion is claimed.

people.facts: Temujin’s father; Hoelun’s husband; death in the late twelfth century. Exact year differs between the Mongolian lead and infobox.
Temujin’s mother and Yesugei’s wife; she raised the children after his death. Exact lifespan is not agreed across the two biographies.
Temujin/Genghis Khan; parents Yesugei and Hoelun; title and imperial foundation in 1206; died in 1227. Retain approximate birth year and no exact death day.
Genghis Khan’s principal wife; mother of Jochi, Chagatai, Ogedei and Tolui. Family and political role supported.
Borte’s eldest son, accepted by Genghis Khan; father of Batu and Berke. English death discussion gives 1225 or 1227, while Mongolian uses circa 1225 and 1225–1226 elsewhere.
Second son of Genghis Khan and Borte; Central Asian appanage; death in 1242.
Third son of Genghis Khan and Borte; elected in 1229 after Tolui’s regency; ruled until 1241. Use the Mongolian revision preceding the anomalous October edit.
Ogedei’s wife and Guyuk’s mother; administration between Ogedei’s death and Guyuk’s election. Leads use 1241–1246; infoboxes distinguish formal regency from 1242.
Fourth son of Genghis Khan and Borte; husband of Sorghaghtani; father of Mongke, Kublai, Hulegu and Ariq; regent during 1227–1229, later honored posthumously.
Tolui’s wife and mother of Mongke, Kublai, Hulegu and Ariq. Birth is placed in the late twelfth century; death in 1252.
Son of Ogedei and Toregene; reign 1246–1248, followed by Oghul Qaimish’s regency.
Son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani; reign 1251–1259; accession transferred the supreme title to Tolui’s line. Birth and exact coronation dates conflict inside the Mongolian page.
Son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani; born 1215, died 1294; rival elections in 1260; Great Yuan name in 1271; Southern Song defeated in 1279.
Kublai’s wife, Zhenjin’s mother; died in 1281. Political and religious influence supported; birth precision not increased.
Son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani; separately elected in 1260; war with Kublai ended with submission in 1264. Do not import judgments of exclusive legitimacy.
Son of Kublai and Chabi; father of Temur and Darmabala; died before Kublai. Crown-prince year is 1273 in English/Yuan shi versus 1274 in Mongolian.
Zhenjin’s third son and Kublai’s grandson; reign 1294–1307; brother of Darmabala.
Zhenjin’s second son; Temur’s elder brother; father of Qaishan. The posthumous imperial honor remains supported by English/Yuan shi, not established by the inspected Mongolian biography.
Darmabala’s son and Temur’s nephew; reign 1307–1311; father of Kusala.
Qaishan’s eldest son and Toghon Temur’s father; brief reign in 1329. Exact days vary within the Mongolian text; retain year precision.
Kusala’s son; reign began 1333; withdrew from Dadu in 1368; died 1370 and was succeeded by Ayushiridara. Describe the capital’s loss without asserting one uniform territorial endpoint.
Keraite ruler; Yesugei’s anda and Temujin’s early patron, later adversary.
Temujin’s anda, ally in the Merkit episode and later political/military rival.
Jochi’s son; supported Mongke’s accession. English describes the 1250/1251 election sequence; Mongolian supporting passages are less specific.
Son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani; campaign ordered by Mongke; founded the Ilkhanate; died 1265. English/Mongolian campaign-start dates differ (1253 mobilization versus 1255 dispatch).
Jochi’s son and Golden Horde ruler; war with Hulegu in 1262–1263. Keep the 1266/1267 end-date uncertainty; do not infer a direct succession from Batu.
Khabul’s father in the recorded genealogy. Exact dates and expanded Timurid genealogical traditions remain uncertain.
Tumbinai’s son, Bartan’s father and ruler of Khamag Mongol; Ambaghai succeeded him. Conflicting claims about other descendants are not imported.
Khabul’s son and Yesugei’s father. English evidence is in Yesugei/Khabul biographies, since the English Bartan title redirects to Yesugei.
Toghon Temur’s son; reign 1370–1378; Maidarbal’s father. Mongolian birth years disagree internally, so no exact birth year is added.

Ayushiridara’s son; captured by Ming forces in 1370 and returned north in 1374. English Maidilibala and Mongolian Ayushiridara support these episodes unevenly; identification with Elbeg remains a hypothesis.
Founder and emperor of Ming, reign 1368–1398. The two biographies do not establish the exact 1370 letter; existing Ming records remain necessary.
Xiongnu chanyu; reign 209–174 BCE and consolidation of steppe groups. Birth is approximate, c.234 BCE. No identification of Xiongnu with a modern ethnic group is asserted.

events.note: Poisoning tradition and late-twelfth-century placement agree; retain period precision because exact years differ.
Title and imperial foundation in 1206 agree.
Regency began after Genghis Khan’s death in 1227 and ended in 1229.
1229 election agrees with English and the reviewed Mongolian old revision.
1241–1246 describes the post-Ogedei interval; both infoboxes start formal regency in 1242. Retain the broad interval, not an exact accession day.
Accession in 1246 agrees.
1251 accession and Toluid succession agree. Berke’s specific role is supported by English and existing primary/scholarly sources; not established by the inspected Mongolian passages.

English describes mobilization in 1253 and arrival in Transoxiana in 1255; Mongolian dates Mongke’s dispatch to 1255. The 1253 departure statement is not bilingually confirmed; retain the existing Yuan shi/Iranica sources for adjudication. Iranica was re-read: it explicitly dates departure to 1253 and arrival in Transoxania to 1255, supporting the existing wording.
Rival elections and war from 1260 to 1264 agree; omit judgments of one side’s exclusive legitimacy.
1262–1263 fighting agrees; the possible winter 1261–1262 start and relative weight of territorial/revenue causes still rely on existing Iranica scholarship.
Great Yuan dynastic name proclaimed in 1271 agrees.
Defeat of Southern Song in 1279 agrees.
Temur’s accession in 1294 after Kublai agrees; his father died before Kublai.
1368 withdrawal from Dadu and continuation of Toghon Temur’s reign until 1370 agree. Replaced the geographically overbroad statement.
Accession after his father’s death in 1370 agrees; do not add an exact day.
English Maidilibala records capture in Yingchang in 1370; Mongolian Ayushiridara identifies his captive son on release, without dating the capture. Existing Ming record retained.
The precise letter and its contents are not located in the two biographies. Keep the existing Ming Taizu shilu volume 57 citation; do not mark Wikipedia verification complete.
English Maidilibala and Mongolian Ayushiridara both record release/return in 1374; autumn detail remains tied to the existing Ming citation.
Modu became Xiongnu chanyu in 209 BCE and consolidated steppe groups. This is regional background, not a modern ethnic identity claim.
Tanshihuai consolidated the Xianbei in the second century. English overview variants use 147/mid-second century; Mongolian uses 156. Keep century precision.
Shelun/Jarun assumed the khagan title in 402.
Bumin defeated Rouran forces; the First Turkic Khaganate was established in 552.

Shiwei was a historical umbrella name for northeastern Asian groups; records include Menggu Shiwei. Do not equate every Shiwei group with later Mongols. Broad attestation period; the composition and identification of individual groups are debated.
The Uyghur Khaganate formed in 744, with Ordu-Baliq as its centre in the Orkhon valley.
Yenisei Kyrgyz forces destroyed Ordu-Baliq in 840; Uyghur groups dispersed west and south.
Abaoji founded the Khitan-led dynastic state in 916, conventionally known as Liao; its influence extended into the steppe.
The twelfth-century Khamag Mongol confederation occupied the Onon/Kherlen region; Khabul was one of its early recorded rulers.
A coalition opposed to Temujin elected Jamukha Gur Khan in 1201.
The alliance between Toghrul and Temujin broke down; Temujin defeated the Keraites in 1203.
Temujin defeated the Naimans under Tayang Khan in 1204, preceding the unification of 1206.

Mongolian writing adapted from Old Uyghur was adopted for state records around 1204; tradition associates this with Tata-tonga. Circa 1204 is a conventional adoption date; distinguish adaptation/use from an exact invention day.
The 1209–1210 campaign ended with Western Xia submission in 1210.
The Mongol–Jin war began in 1211 and continued in stages until 1234.
Mongol forces captured the Jin capital Zhongdu, in the area of modern Beijing, in 1215.

The initial campaign of 1219–1221 captured Bukhara and Samarkand and caused severe civilian destruction. The Mongolian page includes subsequent campaigns through 1231; this event covers the initial campaign only.
Jebe and Subutai defeated a coalition of Rus and Cuman/Kipchak forces at the Kalka River in 1223.
Western Xia fell in 1227 after the final Mongol campaign; Genghis Khan died in the same year. Year only; the English campaign page contains a conflicting death-month statement, which is not used.
Mongol and Southern Song forces captured Caizhou; the Jin dynasty ended in 1234.
Ogedei developed Karakorum and built the Tumen Amgalan palace in 1235–1236. Sources distinguish construction in 1235 and completion/celebration in 1236; use a range.
Batu/Subutai campaigns reached Volga Bulgaria, Rus, Poland and Hungary; the main army withdrew from central Europe in 1242.

The Secret History is a thirteenth-century Mongolian historical/literary work about Genghis Khan and the reign of Ogedei. Compilation date is disputed among several Year-of-the-Rat dates; retain thirteenth-century precision.
The Jochid ulus developed around the lower Volga under Batu; later known as the Golden Horde. Broad development period, not a single foundation day.
The Ilkhanate developed from Hulegu’s conquests in Iran from 1256.
Hulegu’s forces captured Baghdad in 1258, ending Abbasid rule there; the city suffered destruction and mass killing.
Mamluk forces defeated Kitbuqa’s Mongol army at Ain Jalut in 1260, checking the regional advance.
Yuan forces attempted two invasions of Japan, in 1274 and 1281; neither achieved conquest. Two separate campaigns; the slash-separated display avoids suggesting continuous war between the dates.
The Ilkhanate fragmented after Abu Sa’id died in 1335; no unsupported cause of death is asserted.
The Chagatai realm divided into western Transoxiana and eastern Moghulistan in the mid-fourteenth century, conventionally dated 1347.
Ming forces under Lan Yu defeated Toghus Temur’s camp near Buir Lake in 1388; the khan escaped and many people were captured.
Esen’s Oirat army defeated Ming forces at Tumu and captured the Zhengtong emperor in 1449.
Esen assumed the khagan title in 1453; his tenure was brief. Exact end/death years differ across article fields; no precise death date is included.

Dayan Khan and Mandukhai worked to reunify the Mongol tumens; the six-tumen order developed during his reign. Birth/accession chronology varies. Display a broad fifteenth–sixteenth-century period; 1480–1517 is an ordering interval, not a claim that unification happened in one year.
Crimean forces ended the Great Horde, the Golden Horde’s rump state, in 1502; other Jochid successor khanates continued.

Altan’s forces reached Beijing’s outskirts in 1550 amid conflict over trade with Ming. Mongolian wording sometimes says Beijing was taken; English specifies the suburbs/siege. Use outskirts, not capture of the imperial city.
The 1571 Altan–Ming settlement enabled expanded frontier trade.
Altan conferred the Dalai Lama title on Sonam Gyatso in 1578, influencing the spread of Tibetan Buddhism among Mongols.

Erdene Zuu was founded near Karakorum under Abtai in 1585–1586 and became an important religious centre. Construction/foundation dates are described as 1585 and 1586 in different accounts; retain the range.
Ligdan died in 1634 while moving toward Qinghai; Chakhar authority weakened.

Hong Taiji proclaimed Qing in 1636; many Inner Mongol princes recognized his authority. This is distinct from Khalkha’s later incorporation. Do not copy the Mongolian overview’s erroneous statement dating Ligdan’s death to 1636.
Khalkha and Oirat rulers adopted the Mongol–Oirat code in 1640, covering mutual obligations and social rules.

At the 1691 Dolon Nor assembly, Khalkha leaders accepted Qing authority and the banner administration was extended to Khalkha. The Dolon Nor assembly itself is explicitly identified in the English and Mongolian Zanabazar biographies.
Qing forces defeated Galdan at Jao Modo/Zuunmod in 1696; he withdrew with his remaining forces.

The Qing conquest ended the Dzungar state in 1755–1758; Qing military mass killing, war and disease devastated the population. The core sequence and mass killing are supported in both versions. Population estimates differ; no numerical death toll is adopted.
Outer Mongolian leaders declared independence from Qing and enthroned the Bogd Jebtsundamba in 1911; this describes the declaration, not universal recognition.
Russia, China and Mongolia signed the 1915 Kyakhta treaty recognizing Outer Mongolian autonomy under Chinese suzerainty.
events.peopleLinkNote: Bogd is linked as ruler of the state whose autonomy the treaty recognized, not as a claim that he personally signed it.

events.note: The Republic of China’s Beiyang government revoked Outer Mongolia’s autonomy in 1919 and imposed military control.
Mongolian revolutionaries with Soviet Red Army support took Urga in 1921; a new government retained the Bogd as a limited monarch.
After the Bogd’s death, the first constitution and Mongolian People’s Republic were proclaimed in 1924.
events.peopleLinkNote: The event explicitly refers to Bogd’s death before proclamation of the republic; the link does not make him a participant in the later proclamation.

events.note: Political repression intensified in the Mongolian People’s Republic in 1937–1939; monks, intellectuals and other citizens were executed or imprisoned. Both versions describe the 1937–1939 peak; overall period and death estimates differ, so no death total is used.
Mongolian and Soviet forces fought Japan and Manchukuo at Khalkhin Gol in 1939; a Soviet–Mongolian victory was followed by an autumn ceasefire.
The Mongolian People’s Republic began introducing Cyrillic in 1941; implementation in education/administration was gradual.
An independence referendum was held in 1945; the Republic of China government recognized Outer Mongolian independence in early 1946. No electoral percentage is asserted.
The Inner Mongolia autonomous government was established on 1 May 1947, initially based in Ulanhot.
The People’s Republic of China and Mongolian People’s Republic established diplomatic relations in 1949.
The Mongolian People’s Republic joined the United Nations in 1961.
The 1989–1990 protests and hunger strikes led to a transition toward multiparty politics and the 1990 multiparty election.
The 1992 constitution established the name Mongolia and a constitutional framework for multiparty democracy and rights.
The Democratic Union Coalition won the 1996 parliamentary election, producing the first non-MPRP government since 1921.
The Mongolian government and project partners signed the Oyu Tolgoi investment agreement in 2009, a major mining-sector milestone.

China and Mongolia elevated relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2014. The Mongolian article dates the comprehensive strategic partnership to 2014. The inspected English bilateral-relations article establishes the partnership but does not give its 2014 inception date. The 2022 official joint statement explicitly recalls the 2014 founding declaration.
Following the 2023 constitutional amendment, the 2024 election was the first for a 126-member State Great Khural.
